content: BMI-1, also referred to as polycomb group RING finger protein 4 (PCGF4) or RING finger protein 51 (RNF51), is a protein encoded by the BMI1 gene in humans. The BMI1 gene is also known as the B cell-specific Moloney murine leukemia virus integration site 1. BMI-1 is classified as a polycomb RING finger oncogene. BMI-1 has been identified as an oncogene due to its role in regulating the cell cycle inhibitor genes p16 and p19. In mice, the knockout of the Bmi1 gene results in significant defects in hematopoiesis, skeletal patterning, neurological functions, and cerebellar development. Recent studies have shown that BMI-1 is rapidly recruited to sites of DNA damage and remains there for over 8 hours. The loss of BMI-1 leads to increased sensitivity to radiation and impaired repair of DNA double-strand breaks via homologous recombination. BMI-1 is essential for efficient self-renewing cell divisions in adult hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and neural stem cells (NSCs) in both the peripheral and central nervous systems. However, it is less critical for the generation of differentiated progeny. Given the wide range of phenotypic changes observed in Bmi1 knockout mice and its broad tissue distribution, it is hypothesized that BMI-1 may regulate the self-renewal of other types of somatic stem cells. Additionally, BMI-1 is thought to inhibit neuronal aging by suppressing the activity of p53. BMI-1 expression interacts with several key signaling pathways, including Wnt, Akt, Notch, Hedgehog, and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) pathways. In the context of Ewing sarcoma family tumors (ESFT), the knockdown of the BMI1 gene significantly affects the Notch and Wnt signaling pathways, which are critical for the formation and progression of ESFT. BMI-1 has also been shown to mediate the effects of the Hedgehog signaling pathway on mammary stem cell proliferation. Furthermore, BMI-1 regulates multiple downstream factors and genes, including the repression of p19Arf and p16Ink4a. Neural stem cells and HSCs lacking BMI-1 exhibit high expression levels of p19Arf and p16Ink4a, which reduces their proliferation rates. BMI-1 is also implicated as a key factor in controlling Th2 cell differentiation and development by stabilizing GATA transcription factors. The BMI1 gene spans approximately 4 kilobases, contains 10 exons, and is highly conserved across species. The BMI-1 protein consists of 326 amino acids and has a molecular weight of 36,949 Da. Structurally, BMI-1 contains a RING finger domain at its N-terminus and a central helix-turn-helix domain. The RING finger domain is cysteine-rich and involved in zinc binding, contributing to the ubiquitination process. The interaction between BMI-1 and Ring1B significantly enhances the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity. Both the RING domain and the extended N-terminal tail are essential for the interaction between BMI-1 and Ring1B. Clinically, the overexpression of BMI-1 has been implicated in various cancers, including bladder, skin, prostate, breast, ovarian, colorectal cancers, and hematological malignancies. Its amplification and overexpression are particularly pronounced in mantle cell lymphomas. Inhibiting BMI-1 has been shown to suppress the proliferation of glioblastoma multiforme, chemoresistant ovarian cancer, prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, and skin cancers. In colorectal cancer, BMI-1 inhibition reduces the self-renewal capacity of cancer stem cells. In mouse xenograft models, colon cancer stem cells were effectively eliminated by inhibiting the BMI1 gene, suggesting a novel therapeutic approach for colorectal cancer. According to research conducted by Canadian scientists, the loss of BMI1 gene expression in human neurons may play a direct role in the development of Alzheimer’s disease.
